title: You Are My Portion: The Path of Life
summary: David asks God to keep him and confesses that he has no good apart from the LORD. He delights in God's people, refuses the worship of other gods, and rejoices that the LORD is his portion and his inheritance. Because God is always before him and at his right hand, he is unshaken, and he trusts that God will not abandon him to Sheol but will show him the path of life and fill him with joy in his presence.
story: Psalm 15 asked who may dwell with God. Psalm 16 is the voice of such a person, speaking not about moral conditions but about love: the LORD is his good, his portion, his cup, his counselor, and his joy. The psalm is one of the brightest expressions of trust in Book 1, and it pushes the hope of the Psalter further than any psalm before it. Earlier laments feared that death would end praise (Psalm 6:5). Psalm 16 dares to hope that God will not abandon his faithful one to the grave. The New Testament will treat that hope as a prophecy of the resurrection.
historical:
The heading calls the psalm a Miktam of David. The same term heads Psalms 56 to 60, most of which are tied to crises in David's life, but Psalm 16 gives no occasion. Its setting may be a time of danger (verse 1 asks God to preserve him), and some readers connect verse 4's rejection of other gods with David's complaint that his enemies had driven him from the LORD's inheritance and effectively told him to go and serve other gods (1 Samuel 26:19). Others read the psalm as a general confession of loyalty with no particular crisis behind it.

The apostles took the Davidic heading seriously. In Acts 2:25-31, Peter quotes verses 8 to 11 and argues that David could not have been speaking only of himself, since David died, was buried, and his tomb was still known in Jerusalem. Paul makes a similar argument in Acts 13:35-37. Modern scholars differ on whether the psalm originally expressed hope for rescue from an early death or hope beyond death itself, but its later reading as a resurrection text was decisive for the early church.
cultural:
Verses 5 and 6 draw on Israel's system of land ownership. When Israel entered Canaan, the land was divided among the tribes and families by lot (Joshua 14 to 19), and boundary lines were measured with a cord. Each family's allotment was its inheritance, passed down through the generations. The priests and Levites, however, received no tribal territory; the LORD himself was their portion and inheritance (Numbers 18:20; Deuteronomy 10:9). The psalmist takes that priestly privilege as his own: God is the share of land, the cup, and the lot that has fallen to him. The “cup” may reflect the practice of a host assigning a guest's cup at a meal.

Verse 4 refers to the worship of other gods with drink offerings, poured liquid offerings that were part of worship in Israel and among its neighbors. The mention of blood may suggest pagan rites or offerings associated with violence; the details are uncertain. Verse 7 says that at night his “conscience” instructs him; the Hebrew literally says his kidneys, which stood for the innermost self. Verse 8's “right hand” was the place of a protector or advocate, and at a king's right hand was the place of honor.
literary: Psalm 16 is a psalm of trust and confession. It opens with a prayer and a confession of God as the psalmist's only good (verses 1 and 2), then speaks of two groups of people: the faithful in whom he delights and the worshipers of other gods whom he refuses to join (verses 3 and 4). The center celebrates God as his portion (verses 5 and 6), and the rest of the psalm moves outward in widening confidence: God counsels him (verse 7), stands at his right hand (verse 8), keeps him in life and beyond death (verses 9 and 10), and will fill him with joy forever (verse 11). The phrase “right hand” appears at the psalm's turning point (verse 8) and at its close (verse 11). Verses 3 and 4 are among the hardest in the Psalms to translate; the Hebrew is compressed, and versions differ significantly.

outline.t: Heading and confession: no good apart from you
Delight in the saints, refusal of other gods
The LORD is my portion and inheritance
Counsel by night, the LORD at my right hand
Not abandoned to Sheol: the path of life

doctrines.note: The psalm hopes that God will not abandon his faithful one to Sheol and will show him the path of life. The New Testament reads this hope as fulfilled in the resurrection of Jesus and extended to all who belong to him.
Verse 4 refuses the worship of other gods and warns that those who chase them multiply their sorrows. Loyalty to God is exclusive, and its reward is God himself.

Peter and Paul both argue that the psalm speaks of the Messiah's resurrection, since David himself saw decay. The church confesses that Christ rose bodily from the dead, the Holy One whom God did not abandon to the grave.

words.note: Cheleq, portion or share. The word describes a share of plunder, food, or land. In Numbers 18:20 God tells Aaron that he will have no portion among the tribes because the LORD himself is his portion. The psalmist claims that same privilege: God is his share.

Chasid, faithful or holy one. In verse 10 it is rendered “Your Holy One”. The word describes someone who is loyal to God's covenant love. Peter's sermon in Acts 2 applies this title to Jesus, the faithful one who was not left to decay.

Shachat, pit or corruption. The word can mean the pit of the grave or the decay of the body in it. The Greek translation rendered it as corruption, and the apostles' argument in Acts depends on that sense: David's body decayed, but Jesus' did not. Translations of the Hebrew vary between pit and decay.

christ: This is one of the most important psalms for the New Testament's proclamation of the resurrection. On the day of Pentecost Peter quotes verses 8 to 11 (Acts 2:25-28) and argues that David, being a prophet and knowing God's promise to seat one of his descendants on his throne, foresaw the resurrection of the Messiah (Acts 2:29-31). Paul makes the same argument in Pisidian Antioch, quoting verse 10 (Acts 13:35-37). Here the New Testament presents the psalm not merely as a pattern but as prophecy. The church's first-order confession, that Jesus rose bodily from the dead, stands behind the apostles' reading, and Christians see in verse 11 the life of the world to come, joy in God's presence forever.

hard.q: Did David mean this psalm as a prophecy of resurrection, or did the apostles read that into it?
hard.a: Some scholars argue that David originally meant only that God would keep him from an untimely death, and that the apostles read the psalm in a new light after Easter. Others argue that the language of verses 10 and 11, with its talk of Sheol, decay, the path of life, and eternal pleasures, already points beyond this life, and that Peter was drawing out its full sense when he called David a prophet. A third view holds that the psalm expressed a real but open-ended hope that only the resurrection of Jesus made clear. All three views agree that the apostles read the psalm as fulfilled in Christ and that the church's confession of the resurrection does not depend on David's full understanding of his own words.

questions: Verse 2 says “apart from You I have no good thing.” What are you tempted to treat as your real good instead of God?
The Levites had no land because the LORD was their portion. What would it mean for God to be your inheritance, even if you lost something you value?
How does the hope of the resurrection in verses 10 and 11 change the way you face death, your own or that of someone you love?
